topic.subject: further-maths
topic.examWeightHint: Unit 2 is one hour and fifty marks over six questions, sat every Summer. Resolving is a step inside a longer forces question rather than a question of its own, and it appears in two or three of the six questions every year, usually for 2 or 3 marks a part. The reports name the sine and cosine mix-up in almost every series, which makes these the marks most often thrown away by candidates who understand the mechanics.
mustMemorise: Component along a line = F cos of the angle between the force and that line
Component at right angles to it = F sin of the same angle
On a slope of angle a: mg sin a down the slope, mg cos a into it
Turn a mass into a weight with g = 10 before resolving
A component that points the other way is subtracted
notOnThisSpec: Resolving in two directions that are not at right angles to each other
The coefficient of friction and F = μR: a frictional force is given, as a number or as so many newtons per kilogram

sheet.howExamined: Unit 2, one hour, fifty marks, six questions, calculator allowed, formula sheet on page 2. Resolving sits inside a longer forces question and carries 2 or 3 marks a part: Summer 2025 Q6(ii) asked for the normal reaction on a slope for 2, Summer 2023 Q3(i) and (ii) for 2 each, and Summer 2024 Q3(i) and (ii) for 3 each where two angled forces had to be resolved before an equation could be written. The scheme gives MW for a correct resolved component and W for the value, with follow-through into the parts that use it.
traps: Sine and cosine interchanged, the error the reports name year after year (Summer 2024 Q3, Summer 2025 Q6(ii), Summer 2022 Q3(b)(ii))
An angle measured from the wrong line, so a force given at an angle to the vertical or to the plane is resolved as though it were given to the horizontal (Summer 2024 Q3)
A force left unresolved, with its whole magnitude put into the working (Summer 2024 Q3)
The magnitude of a force and its angle mixed up when resolving (Summer 2024 Q3)
g left out, so the mass is resolved instead of the weight (Summer 2019 Q3(ii))
A component that acts the other way added instead of subtracted (Summer 2022 Q3(b)(ii), Summer 2024 Q3)

noteBlocks.lede: A rope that pulls at an angle is doing two jobs at once: dragging along the floor and lifting. Resolving splits one slanted force into those two straight ones, so the rest of the mechanics can be done a direction at a time.
can: Split a force at an angle into a component along a line and one at right angles to it
Resolve the weight of a body on a slope into its two components
Read which angle to use, and which line it is measured from

noteBlocks.md: Pull a suitcase by its handle and some of your pull drags it forwards while some lifts it. Splitting that one pull into a forwards part and an upwards part is what resolving does.

noteBlocks.caption: One slanted pull replaced by two at right angles.

noteBlocks.md: Drop a dashed line from the tip of the force onto the line you care about. The force is now the longest side of a right-angled triangle, and the two shorter sides are its components: the side beside the angle uses cosine, the side opposite uses sine.

**Along the floor:** $46\cos 22° = 42.65$ N, the side beside the angle.
**Upwards:** $46\sin 22° = 17.23$ N, the side opposite it.

noteBlocks.prompt: A rope pulls a sledge with a force of 25 N at 40° to the ground. What is the part of the pull along the ground, in newtons, to 2 decimal places?
noteBlocks.explain: The ground is beside the $40°$ angle, so it takes the cosine, as the floor did above: $25\cos 40° = 19.15$ N. The sine would give the part lifting the sledge.

noteBlocks.text: 2. Why cosine goes with the angle

noteBlocks.title: Why cosine shortens the force
noteBlocks.md: Think of the arrow's shadow on the line. When the force lies along the line there is no tilt, $\cos 0° = 1$, and the whole force counts. Turn it to a right angle and the shadow vanishes. Cosine is the fraction of the force that survives the turn.

**Shown, a 50 N force:** at $60°$ to the line, $50\cos 60° = 50 \times 0.5 = 25$ N survives.
**At $90°$:** $50\cos 90° = 50 \times 0 = 0$: none of it acts along the line.

noteBlocks.prompt: A force of 20 N acts at 60° to a straight line. What is its component along that line, in newtons?
noteBlocks.explain: Half the force survives a turn of $60°$, as for the 50 N force above: $20\cos 60° = 20 \times 0.5 = 10$ N.

noteBlocks.caption: The weight split down the slope and into it.

noteBlocks.md: On a slope the useful directions are along the surface and at right angles to it, so the weight is the force to split. The angle between the weight and the line into the slope is the slope's own angle $\alpha$, so into the slope is $mg\cos\alpha$ and down the slope is $mg\sin\alpha$.

**Weight first:** $11 \times 10 = 110$ N.
**Down the slope:** $110\sin 30° = 55$ N; **into it:** $110\cos 30° = 95.26$ N.

noteBlocks.prompt: A box of weight $W$ rests on a slope inclined at $\alpha$ to the horizontal. Which expression gives the component of the weight acting down the slope?
noteBlocks.explain: The slope's angle sits between the weight and the line into the surface, so the cosine part goes into the slope and the sine part runs down it, as for the 11 kg box above.

noteBlocks.text: 4. Which line the angle is measured from

noteBlocks.alt: A box on a slope inclined at 21 degrees, pulled by a rope with a force of 75 N at 32 degrees to the slope itself. The slope's direction is continued as a dashed line from the box, and the 32 degree angle is marked between it and the rope.

noteBlocks.caption: An angle given to the slope, not to the horizontal.

noteBlocks.md: A question may give the angle to the horizontal, to the vertical, or to the slope itself. Only the angle between the force and the direction you are resolving along belongs in the cosine.

**Shown:** the rope is $32°$ from the slope, so along the slope it gives $75\cos 32° = 75 \times 0.848 = 63.60$ N.
**Not:** $32°$ from the horizontal, which would resolve along the wrong line.

noteBlocks.prompt: A rope pulls a box up a slope. The rope is at 32° to the slope, and the slope is at 21° to the horizontal. Which angle is used for the component of the pull along the slope?
noteBlocks.explain: The component along the slope needs the angle between the rope and the slope, which the question gives directly as $32°$, as in the line above.

noteBlocks.alt: A point O pulled by 36 N horizontally to the right and 14 N up and to the left at 60 degrees to the horizontal, with dashed reference lines through O.

noteBlocks.caption: Two pulls whose horizontal parts face each other.

noteBlocks.md: A component has a direction as well as a size. Choose one way along the line as positive; a component pointing the other way is then negative, and it is subtracted rather than added.

**Shown:** the 14 N pull gives $14\cos 60° = 7$ N to the left, which is $-7$ N.
**To the right in total:** $36 - 7 = 29$ N, not $36 + 7 = 43$ N.

noteBlocks.prompt: A force of 16 N acts at 60° above the horizontal, to the left. Taking to the right as positive, which is its horizontal component?
noteBlocks.explain: Its size is $16\cos 60° = 8$ N, and it points left, the negative way, as the 14 N pull did above: $-8$ N.

noteBlocks.md: **An angle to the vertical** (2024, 2026). Now the vertical part is beside the angle, so it takes the cosine, and the horizontal part the sine.

**Shown:** 18 N at $25°$ to the vertical: vertically $18\cos 25° = 16.31$ N.
**Horizontally:** $18\sin 25° = 7.61$ N.

noteBlocks.prompt: A force of P newtons acts at 30° to the vertical. Which expression gives its vertical component?
noteBlocks.explain: Measured from the vertical, the vertical side is beside the angle, so it takes the cosine, as the 18 N force above did.

noteBlocks.md: **A mass, not a weight** (2023, 2025). The question gives the mass; the weight $mg$ is what gets resolved. **Shown:** a 3 kg parcel on a 30° slope: $3 \times 10 = 30$ N first, then $30\sin 30° = 15$ N down the slope.

noteBlocks.prompt: A crate of mass 12 kg rests on a slope inclined at 30° to the horizontal. What is the component of its weight acting down the slope, in newtons?
noteBlocks.explain: Weight first, as for the parcel above: $12 \times 10 = 120$ N. Then $120\sin 30° = 60$ N down the slope.

noteBlocks.md:
Split any force into a component along a line and one at right angles to it.
Resolve the weight on a slope into mg sine and mg cosine of the slope's angle.
Pick out which angle the question gives, and which line it is measured from.
Combine components that point opposite ways by subtracting.

Resolving is rarely asked for on its own: it sits inside 'Calculate the normal reaction' or 'Calculate the value of P', worth 2 to 4 marks. The first mark is for a correct resolved component written down; the last is for the value, to 2 decimal places. Stuck? Draw the right-angled triangle, mark the angle, and ask which side of it you want.

workedExamples.stem:
A sledge is pulled along level ground by a rope. The pull along the rope is $42$ N and the rope makes an angle of $28°$ with the ground.

Calculate the component of the pull
(i) parallel to the ground,
(ii) at right angles to the ground.

Round each answer to 2 decimal places.

figure.alt: A sledge pulled along level ground by a rope with a force of 42 N at 28 degrees to the ground.

steps.working: The pull, the ground and the dashed vertical make a right-angled triangle with the $28°$ angle at the sledge.
steps.decision: Draw the triangle before choosing a ratio: the angle has to be marked between the force and the line you are resolving along.

options: Because the ratio depends on which side of the angle the direction lies
Because the triangle gives the size of the force
Because the angle must always be measured from the horizontal
whyMenu.explain: The force is known already. What the triangle settles is which of its two shorter sides you want, and that is what fixes sine or cosine.

steps.decision: The ground is the side beside the angle, so this component takes the cosine.

steps.working: At right angles to the ground: $42\sin 28° = 19.72$ N.
steps.decision: The upward direction is opposite the angle, so this one takes the sine.

steps.working: Check: the size of the pull is $\sqrt{37.08^2 + 19.72^2} = 42.00$ N.
steps.decision: The two components are the legs of a right-angled triangle whose longest side is the force, so Pythagoras is a free check.

workedExamples.stem:
A box of mass $9$ kg rests on a slope inclined at $24°$ to the horizontal.

Calculate the component of the weight of the box
(i) down the slope,
(ii) at right angles to the slope.

Round each answer to 2 decimal places.

figure.alt: A box of mass 9 kg resting on a slope inclined at 24 degrees, with its weight of 90 N drawn straight down.

steps.decision: Turn the mass into a force first: a component of a mass means nothing, and g = 10 on this paper.

steps.working: The angle between the weight and the line into the slope is the slope's own angle: $\theta = 24°$.
steps.decision: The two right angles in the picture force it: tilt the surface by 24° and the normal tilts by 24° as well.
Down the slope is opposite that angle, so it takes the sine.
Into the slope sits beside the angle, so it takes the cosine. It is the larger of the two for any slope under 45°.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: in a right-angled triangle, which ratio connects the angle to the side next to it and the longest side?

options.feedback: Cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, so it reaches the side beside the angle.
Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, so it reaches the side across from the angle.
Tangent connects the two shorter sides and leaves the longest one out.
That relates the three sides but uses no angle at all.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: work out $30\cos 60°$.

options.feedback: $\cos 60° = 0.5$, so the answer is half of 30.
That leaves the cosine out altogether.
That is $30\sin 60°$.
That is the cosine on its own, without the 30.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: taking $g = 10$ m/s², what is the weight of a body of mass $14$ kg?

options.feedback: That is the mass with newtons written after it.
That divides by $g$ instead of multiplying.
That uses $g = 9.8$, which this unit does not.

items.stem: A force $F$ acts at an angle $\theta$ to a straight line. Which expression gives its component along that line?

options.feedback: The line is the side beside the angle, so the cosine gives the part along it.
That is the component at right angles to the line, opposite the angle.
Tangent compares the two components with each other, not either of them with the force.
A component is never bigger than the force it came from, so it is multiplied, not divided.

items.stem: A body of weight $W$ rests on a slope inclined at $\alpha$ to the horizontal. Which expression gives the component of $W$ at right angles to the slope?

options.feedback: The slope's angle sits between the weight and the line into the surface, so that component takes the cosine.
That is the component down the slope.
The whole weight only presses into the surface when the surface is horizontal.
Tangent would make the component larger than the weight once the slope passes 45°.

items.stem: A force of $32$ N acts at $20°$ to the vertical. Which expression gives its horizontal component?

options.feedback: Measured from the vertical, the horizontal side is opposite the angle, so it takes the sine.
That is the vertical part: the vertical is beside an angle measured from it.
Tangent compares the two components; it gives neither from the force.
The whole force would act horizontally only if it were horizontal.

items.stem: A rope pulls a box up a slope inclined at $30°$ to the horizontal. The rope makes an angle of $20°$ with the slope. What angle does the rope make with the horizontal?

options.feedback: The slope is $30°$ above the horizontal and the rope $20°$ above the slope, so the rope is $30° + 20° = 50°$ above the horizontal.
$20°$ is measured from the slope, not from the horizontal.
The rope lies above the slope, so the two angles add rather than subtract.
$30°$ is the slope's own angle; the rope rises a further $20°$ above it.

items.stem: One pull gives a component of $30$ N to the right and another gives $12$ N to the left. What is the total component to the right?
items.skill: Combining components that face each other

options.feedback: Opposite directions subtract, so $30 - 12 = 18$ N to the right.
Adding treats the second pull as helping the first, when it works against it.
Components are added and subtracted, never multiplied.
That leaves the first component out of the total altogether.

parts.stem:
A rope pulls a trailer with a force of $50$ N at $32°$ to the horizontal.

Calculate the component of the pull parallel to the horizontal. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: The horizontal is the side beside the angle.
Mark the angle between the force and the direction you are resolving along.
parts.workedSolution: Component $= 50\cos 32° = 42.40$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $50\sin 32°$, the component at right angles. The one along the line sits beside the angle, so it takes the cosine.

parts.stem:
Calculate the component of the pull perpendicular to the horizontal. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

findTheMistake.stem: Ciara is resolving a force of $30$ N that acts at $50°$ to the vertical. She wants its horizontal component. Her working:
studentWorking: the component along a line is force times cosine of the angle
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 takes the cosine of an angle measured from the vertical, which gives the vertical component, not the horizontal one. The horizontal is at right angles to the vertical, so it is opposite the $50°$ and takes the sine.
correction: the angle is $50°$, measured from the vertical
the horizontal is at right angles to the vertical, so it is opposite the angle
findTheMistake.feedback: Quoting the rule correctly earns the method mark (M). Before choosing sine or cosine, mark the angle on a sketch and ask which side of it the direction you want lies on: beside the angle takes cosine, across from it takes sine.

findTheMistake.stem: Dara resolves the weight of a box of mass $6$ kg resting on a slope inclined at $40°$. She wants the component down the slope. Her working:
studentWorking: down the slope is opposite the angle, so it takes the sine
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 resolves the mass, $6$ kg, instead of the weight. The weight is $6 \times 10 = 60$ N, and that is the force that has a component down the slope.
correction: the component down the slope takes the sine of the $40°$
findTheMistake.feedback: Choosing the sine earns the method mark. Before resolving, turn every mass into a weight: a component of a force has to come from a force.

prompts.prompt: A force $F$ makes an angle $\theta$ with a line. What is its component along that line?
prompts.answer: F cos of theta: the cosine goes with the direction beside the angle.

prompts.prompt: A force $F$ makes an angle $\theta$ with a line. What is its component at right angles to the line?
prompts.answer: F sin of theta, because that direction is opposite the angle.

prompts.prompt: What is the first thing to do before resolving the weight of a body given as a mass?
prompts.answer: Turn the mass into a weight by multiplying by g, which is 10 on this paper.

prompts.prompt: On a slope inclined at an angle to the horizontal, what are the two components of the weight?
prompts.answer: mg sine of the angle down the slope, and mg cosine of the angle into the slope.

prompts.prompt: A force is given at an angle to the vertical. Which ratio gives its horizontal component?
prompts.answer: Sine, because the horizontal is at right angles to the line the angle is measured from.

prompts.prompt: Two components lie along the same line but point opposite ways. How are they combined?
prompts.answer: By subtracting one from the other, since a component has a direction as well as a size.

prompts.prompt: How can the two components of a force be checked once both are worked out?
prompts.answer: Square them, add, and take the square root: the answer comes back to the size of the original force.
